# Aligners, pseudoaligners and counters {#sec-tools-landscape}

bagPipes makes particular choices: Trim Galore, Salmon, HISAT2, deepTools.
Papers and other pipelines (nf-core/rnaseq, ENCODE, your collaborators')
make different ones. This chapter is a map of the common tools for each
job, what each one **assumes**, and why bagPipes chose what it did, so a
methods section that says "reads were aligned with STAR and counted with
featureCounts" makes sense.

## Three roads from reads to gene counts

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  T["Trimmed reads"] --> G1["Align to the genome<br/>(splice-aware: STAR, HISAT2)"]
  G1 --> G2["Count reads on genes<br/>(featureCounts, HTSeq-count)"]
  T --> P1["Map to the transcriptome<br/>(Salmon, kallisto)"]
  P1 --> P2["Sum transcripts to genes<br/>(tximport)"]
  G1 --> H1["Genome alignments projected<br/>onto transcripts → Salmon / RSEM"]
  G2 & P2 & H1 --> D["Count matrix → DESeq2 / edgeR / limma"]
```

| Road | Example | Gives you genome tracks? | Handles isoforms? | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Align + count | STAR → featureCounts | yes | no (gene-level only; ambiguous reads dropped) | slower |
| 2. Pseudoalign / quasi-map | **Salmon → tximport** (bagPipes) | no | yes | fast |
| 3. Hybrid | STAR → Salmon (nf-core/rnaseq default), RSEM | yes | yes | slowest |

bagPipes runs **roads 1 and 2 side by side**: Salmon for the numbers, and
HISAT2 for BAMs and tracks you can look at. It does not count reads from the
BAMs.

## Splice-aware aligners

RNA reads come from **spliced** transcripts, so one read can start in exon 1
and end in exon 2, with thousands of bases of intron between them in the genome.
A **splice-aware** aligner can split a read across an intron (the `N` in
CIGAR). A DNA aligner cannot.

| Tool | Splice-aware | Memory (human) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **STAR** | yes | ~32 GB | Very fast and accurate; ENCODE and nf-core standard. Can count genes itself (`--quantMode GeneCounts`) |
| **HISAT2** | yes | ~8 GB | What bagPipes uses. Hierarchical index makes it small; accuracy close to STAR for typical data |
| TopHat / TopHat2 | yes | | **Obsolete**; replaced by HISAT2. You'll still see it in older papers |
| Bowtie2, BWA-MEM | **no** | | DNA aligners: right for ChIP, ATAC, CUT&RUN, WGS; **wrong for RNA-seq** |
| minimap2 | yes (`-ax splice`) | | For **long reads** (Nanopore, PacBio Iso-Seq) |

**What aligners assume**

- The reference genome is right for your samples (same species and build;
  no large deletions or inversions).
- Introns mostly follow the canonical **GT…AG** motif. Aligners give these a
  bonus, which is also how HISAT2 decides the `XS` strand tag.
- A read that fits several places equally well is a **multi-mapper**. Each
  aligner has rules about how many locations to report (HISAT2 searches for up
  to 5 by default; one is marked primary, the rest secondary) and gives them
  low MAPQ.

## Pseudoaligners (lightweight mappers)

Instead of working out a base-by-base alignment, these tools ask only
**which transcripts a read is compatible with**, then use a statistical model
(EM) to divide reads among isoforms ([Salmon](salmon.qmd)). They are
sometimes called *pseudoaligners*, *quasi-mappers* or *lightweight mappers*.

| Tool | Method | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Salmon** | *Selective alignment*: k-mer matching, then a quick alignment score check | What bagPipes uses. Models GC and sequence bias; can use **decoys** (the genome) to avoid assigning intronic/intergenic reads to transcripts |
| **kallisto** | *Pseudoalignment* on a de Bruijn graph of the transcriptome | Very fast, very low memory. Also the base of single-cell tools (`kallisto bus`) |
| RSEM | EM on real alignments to the transcriptome | Older, slower; used by ENCODE and TCGA |

**What pseudoaligners assume**

- **Every RNA in your sample is in the annotation.** Reads from
  unannotated genes, introns (pre-mRNA) or intergenic regions have nowhere to
  go. They are either left unmapped (lower mapping rate) or, worse, assigned
  to a similar annotated transcript. This is why total-RNA libraries map at
  lower rates than poly-A libraries.
- The fragment length distribution, sequence bias and library type can be
  learned from the data.
- They give **no genome coordinates**, so no BAM to view and no tracks. That's
  the reason bagPipes also runs HISAT2.

## Read counters

After genome alignment (road 1), a counter decides which gene each read
belongs to, using the GTF.

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| **featureCounts** (Subread / Rsubread) | Very fast. Counts read pairs on exons, summed per gene. By default **drops multi-mappers and reads overlapping two genes** |
| **HTSeq-count** | The original; slower. Similar rules ("union" mode by default) |
| STAR `--quantMode GeneCounts` | Same idea, done during alignment; writes three columns (unstranded, sense, antisense) |

**What counters assume**: reads that are ambiguous between genes are best
thrown away; gene-level counts are enough (no isoforms); and you've told them
the right strandedness. A wrong strand setting quietly sends most reads to the
"no feature" bin.

## Strandedness: one library, many names

Every tool has its own name for the same library type. For a **dUTP / TruSeq
Stranded / NEB Directional** paired-end library (read 1 antisense):

| Tool | Setting for dUTP | For unstranded | For read-1-sense kits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salmon `-l` | `ISR` (bagPipes uses `A` = detect it) | `IU` | `ISF` |
| kallisto | `--rf-stranded` | (none) | `--fr-stranded` |
| HISAT2 `--rna-strandness` | `RF` (bagPipes doesn't set it) | (none) | `FR` |
| featureCounts `-s` | `2` | `0` | `1` |
| HTSeq-count `-s` | `reverse` | `no` | `yes` |
| STAR GeneCounts column | 4 | 2 | 3 |
| deepTools `--filterRNAstrand` | assumes dUTP | n/a | the opposite of what you want |
| RSeQC `infer_experiment.py` | `1+-,1-+,2++,2--` dominant | ~50/50 | `1++,1--,2+-,2-+` dominant |

Keep this table handy. It's the most common source of confusion when switching
between pipelines.

## Trimmers

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Trim Galore** | What bagPipes uses. A wrapper around **Cutadapt** that auto-detects the adapter and handles pairs |
| Cutadapt | The underlying engine; full control |
| fastp | Fast all-in-one: trimming, QC report, poly-G trimming (helpful for NovaSeq/NextSeq 2-colour chemistry) |
| Trimmomatic | Older, Java; still common in papers |

Note that both Salmon and STAR cope with some leftover adapter by soft-clipping
or ignoring it, so whether to trim at all is debated. Trimming is cheap and
makes QC easier to interpret, which is why bagPipes does it.

## QC tools

| Tool | What it adds |
|---|---|
| **FastQC** | Per-file read QC (bagPipes) |
| **MultiQC** | Collects every tool's logs into one report (bagPipes) |
| samtools `flagstat` / `idxstats` | Alignment summary, reads per chromosome (bagPipes: flagstat) |
| RSeQC | Strandedness (`infer_experiment.py`), gene-body coverage (3' bias), read distribution (exon/intron/intergenic) |
| Qualimap `rnaseq`, Picard `CollectRnaSeqMetrics` | Similar RNA-specific metrics |

## Differential expression tools (after the pipeline)

| Tool | Model | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **DESeq2** | Negative binomial, shrunken dispersions | The usual choice; takes `tximport` output directly ([Into R](into-r.qmd)) |
| edgeR | Negative binomial | Similar results; flexible for complex designs |
| limma-voom | Linear model on log-CPM with weights | Fast; good with many samples |

All three assume that **most genes don't change** between conditions (that's
how they normalise) and that you have **biological replicates**. With one
sample per condition there is no way to estimate variability, so no valid
p-values.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. A collaborator aligned RNA-seq reads with Bowtie2. What will go wrong?
2. Your total-RNA library has a Salmon mapping rate of 45 %, but HISAT2 aligns
   92 % of reads. Is something broken?
3. You switch from bagPipes to a STAR + featureCounts pipeline for a dUTP
   library. Which `-s` value do you give featureCounts?
4. Why does bagPipes run an aligner at all, if Salmon makes the counts?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. Bowtie2 isn't splice-aware, so reads crossing exon–exon junctions fail to
   align or are soft-clipped. You lose a large share of reads, unevenly
   across genes.
2. Probably not. Total RNA has many intronic (pre-mRNA) reads. They align to the
   genome but have no matching transcript in Salmon's index.
3. `-s 2` (reversely stranded).
4. For genome coordinates: BAMs and bigWig tracks to look at in IGV, and
   alignment QC. Salmon doesn't produce these.
:::
:::
